figures.caption: Figure 1: Budget-controlled recovery routing. After a cheap coding attempt fails, the router uses the problem, verdict, and stderr to score recovery actions. CRC maps a user budget B

Figure 3: Cost–solve-rate frontier on the GPT-5.4-nano holdout test split. Blue circles: CRC operating points at different budget levels B; star marks the unconstrained argmax (λ=0). Gray dashed: binary cascade baseline. Amber diamonds: prompt-only LLM routers (zeroshot, no SFT). Crosses: fixed-action baselines.

Table 1: Routing baselines on the GPT-5.4-nano holdout test split (n=360). Left: fixed-action policies. Right: prompt-only models used as zero-shot routers. Costs are in millidollars; in the right table, parenthesized terms split the cost of the selected recovery action and the prompt-only router call.

Figure 4: CRC frontiers on the TACO difficulty ladder (GPT test set). Blue curves are monotone (escalation helps); red curves are non-monotone (escalation backfires on average for this sub-population). Stars mark the argmax (λ=0) operating point; dots are certified feasible points at increasing λ.

Figure 2: Successful-action structure on the pooled GPT-5.4-NANO calibration and test holdout (n=720). Left: benchmark-level distribution of S(x), grouped by cheap-only, overlapping cheap/escalation, and escalation-only recoveries. Right: mean oracle recovery cost compared with always-escalate, in millidollars per example.
